problem: The claim that the classical model gives 'a much weaker temperature dependence than the measured ρ' is wrong at low temperature. Drude's τ falls as 1/v_rms, so the model predicts ρ ∝ √T. Measured ρ falls as T⁵ at low temperature, which is far faster than √T, so there the model's dependence is much stronger, not weaker. The sentence is only true for the high-temperature part.
fix: Wrong — ρ(T): the model predicts ρ ∝ √T, because τ ∝ 1/v_rms ∝ T⁻¹ᐟ². Measured ρ is nearly linear in T at high temperature (stronger than √T) and falls as T⁵ at low temperature (far faster than √T). Neither regime matches the model.

problem: '(3/2)k_B of energy' has the wrong units. k_B is joules per kelvin, so (3/2)k_B is a heat capacity per electron, not an energy. The energy per electron is (3/2)k_BT. A student can read this as saying each electron carries a fixed energy (3/2)k_B.
fix: Classical equipartition gives every electron an average thermal energy (3/2)k_BT, that is a heat capacity of (3/2)k_B per electron, so metals should have a huge electronic heat capacity.

where: Section 3, paragraph comparing σ with the measured 5.9×10⁷ S/m
problem: The agreement presented as a success of the model is circular: τ = 2.5×10⁻¹⁴ s is itself the value back-calculated from the measured conductivity of copper, so σ must come out close. It is a consistency check, not a prediction.
fix: Copper, with n = 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³ and τ = 2.5×10⁻¹⁴ s, gives σ ≈ 6.0×10⁷ S/m, close to the measured 5.9×10⁷ S/m. Since τ here was itself obtained from that measured value, this is a consistency check. When τ is estimated independently from a classical random speed, the model still lands within a factor of about two.

problem: 'Hundreds of times smaller' overstates the gap. For copper at room temperature the ratio of the classical to the measured electronic heat capacity is about 3T/T_F ≈ 80; for silver and sodium it is smaller still (tens, not hundreds).
fix: ...metals show a value about a hundred times smaller at room temperature (roughly a factor 3T/T_F) that grows linearly with T.
